lessonData.subject: Mathematics
lessonData.tagline: Mastering real-life limits: turn everyday budgets and constraints into powerful mathematical decisions.
lessonData.overview: Everyday situations involving spending limits, carrying capacities, or minimum score targets can be represented accurately using linear inequalities in one variable. Because real-world items like snacks, tickets, or currency notes cannot be divided into arbitrary fractions, we must interpret algebraic boundaries to identify the greatest or least feasible integer solution.

nodes.label: Identify Variables & Constraints
nodes.details: Assign a variable to the unknown quantity and determine whether the limit allows equality (<=, >=) or is strict (<, >).

nodes.label: Formulate Linear Inequality
nodes.details: Translate descriptive phrases like 'at most' into <=, 'at least' into >=, and 'strictly less than' into <.

nodes.label: Solve for the Boundary

chalkNotes.title: Modeling Contextual Constraints with Inequalities
chalkNotes.subtitle: Navigating real-world bounds, strictness, and discrete quantities
chalkNotes.coreRuleOrFormula: Cost Expression <= Budget Limit  ==>  Evaluate greatest integer x in feasible region
bulletPoints: 'At most' / 'Budget of $B' means <= (spending exactly $B is permitted).
'Strictly less than' / 'Under $B' means < (spending $B is not permitted).
Do NOT use standard rounding: if x <= 12.5, rounding up to 13 exceeds the budget (13 * $1.60 = $20.80 > $20). The maximum is 12.
If x < 7 for an integer quantity, the boundary 7 is excluded, meaning the maximum feasible integer is 6.
keyTakeaways: Always check your final integer answer back in the original real-world context to confirm you have not broken the limit.
The boundary sign tells you whether exact values are allowed: solid dot on a number line represents <= or >=, while an open circle represents < or >.

quiz.question: A school bakery sells curry puffs for $1.60 each. Maya has a $20 bill to spend on curry puffs. Which inequality and maximum whole number of curry puffs correctly model her purchase?
options: 1.60x <= 20, yielding a maximum of 12 curry puffs
1.60x <= 20, yielding a maximum of 13 curry puffs by rounding up
1.60x < 20, yielding a maximum of 12 curry puffs
1.60x < 20, yielding a maximum of 11 curry puffs
quiz.explanation: Because Maya has a $20 bill, she can spend up to and including $20, so the constraint is 1.60x <= 20. Solving gives x <= 12.5. Since she cannot purchase half a curry puff and 13 curry puffs would cost $20.80 (exceeding her $20 budget), standard rounding does not apply. The greatest integer satisfying x <= 12.5 is 12.

suggestedQuestions: On a number line representation of an inequality, what is the difference between an open circle and a solid dot?
If a cinema ticket costs $13.50, how do we write an algebraic expression for the total cost of n tickets with a $5 booking fee?
When solving an inequality for a minimum requirement (like passing score or minimum weight), why do we take the ceiling integer instead of the floor integer?

nodes.details: Represents minimum targets required for success, such as fundraising amounts or passing test scores.

main.title: Modeling Budget Constraints
main.why: This visualizes the 'cliff' of a budget limit, showing why we cannot round up to 13 curry puffs.
main.checkQuestion: If 12.5 is our mathematical boundary, why can't we simply round up to 13 to get the answer?

steps.name: Draw the budget line
steps.caption: The line shows how our cost grows as we buy more puffs at $1.60 each.

steps.name: Add the budget boundary
steps.caption: We have $20, so we cannot go above this red line.

steps.name: Check 12 puffs
steps.caption: Buying 12 puffs costs $19.20, which is inside our budget.

steps.name: Check 13 puffs
steps.caption: Buying 13 puffs costs $20.80, which is over our budget limit.

contrast:standard-rounding-on-inequaliti.title: Testing the 13-Curry-Puff Rule
contrast:standard-rounding-on-inequaliti.why: This picture makes the physical impossibility of the 'round up' rule visible by comparing the cost of 13 puffs against the budget limit.
contrast:standard-rounding-on-inequaliti.checkQuestion: If 13 puffs cost $20.80 and our budget is $20, why does the rule 'always round up' fail here?

steps.name: Draw the budget limit
steps.caption: Our budget of $20 is the solid red line.

steps.name: Show the cost curve
steps.caption: Buying more curry puffs increases the cost along the blue line.

steps.name: Check 13 puffs
steps.caption: What happens if we test 13 puffs? The point goes above our budget line.

steps.name: Find the maximum
steps.caption: 12 puffs stays at $19.20, which is under our $20 limit.

steps.name: Final check
steps.caption: Looking at the lines, why is 13 not a valid answer for our wallet?

contrast:standard-rounding-on-inequaliti.focus: Fractional solutions in real-world inequalities should always follow standard rounding rules (e.g., 12.5 rounds up to 13).

contrast:budget-strict-inequality-confus.title: Strict vs Inclusive Inequality
contrast:budget-strict-inequality-confus.why: It shows that a bill of exactly $20 is a valid, reachable outcome, refuting the need for a strict '<' sign.
contrast:budget-strict-inequality-confus.checkQuestion: If your bill is exactly $20.00, which sign includes that amount as a valid payment?

steps.name: Setting the scene
steps.caption: You have a $20 budget and a bill of exactly $20.

steps.name: Testing the strict rule
steps.caption: If we use 1.60x < 20, is the bill allowed?

steps.name: Checking understanding
steps.caption: Compare these. Why does the second rule allow the $20 bill?

contrast:budget-strict-inequality-confus.focus: Budget constraints must always use strict inequality '<' because you cannot spend more than your budget.

apply.title: Gym Membership Budget
apply.why: This diagram helps the learner see the physical constraints of a recurring monthly cost versus a fixed entry fee against a fixed total budget.
apply.checkQuestion: At what point does the cost line cross the budget line, and why does this tell us the maximum number of full months?

steps.name: Draw the budget limit
steps.caption: You have a total budget of $100 for your gym membership.

steps.name: Add the joining fee
steps.caption: The gym charges a fixed $25 joining fee before any months start.

steps.name: Model monthly costs

apply.focus: A gym membership has a one-off joining fee of $25 plus $15 per month. Form an inequality and find the maximum number of full months a student can join with a budget of $100.

visualsDeclined.3d: A 3D model is unnecessary because the constraint of linear inequalities in one variable is best represented as a 1D number line or a 2D graph, which are both flat, standard mathematical visualizations
